questions.title: How do you observe your workload from multiple perspectives?
questions.description: Observability empowers businesses to be proactive rather than reactive. Teams can understand the cause-and-effect relationships within their systems, predicting and helping prevent issues rather than reacting to them. As workloads evolve, revisit and refine the observability strategy, verifying that it remains relevant and effective.

helpfulResource.displayText: Application telemetry is the metrics, logs, and traces your workload emits about its own behavior. Without it, you cannot tell whether a release improved or degraded the experience. When telemetry ties technical signals to business outcomes, you see both system health and whether the workload delivers the results the business expects.

User experience telemetry measures how real people experience your application. _Real user monitoring_ captures what happens in the sessions of actual users, and _synthetic monitoring_ runs scripted interactions on a schedule to test critical paths. Together they show what users experience now and whether important functionality still works when traffic is low.

Every workload depends on components beyond your own code: other services of the workload, internal APIs, shared internal platforms, databases, third-party APIs, DNS, network paths, and managed cloud services. Dependency telemetry measures the health and performance of those components so you can attribute a problem to the right one, inside or outside your architecture. Without it, a failing dependency looks like a defect in whichever service alarmed first, cascading failures arrive as surprises, and you cannot predict what a change will affect.

Distributed tracing follows one request as it moves through the services that handle it. In a distributed system, multiple services handle each user action, so a slowdown or failure in any one of them affects the result. Tracing links each service's work into one end-to-end timeline, so you can see where time is spent or where the request fails.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you derive essential insights from your telemetry?
questions.description: Amazon CloudWatch provides the metrics, logs, dashboards, and alarms these practices build on. Amazon CloudWatch Application Signals, when enabled, adds a service-level view of each service's RED metrics (rate, errors, and duration) and the service level objectives (SLOs) that track them, and AWS X-Ray is the trace backend for following individual requests. Together these services turn collected telemetry into the insights that inform data-driven decisions.

helpfulResource.displayText: Key performance indicators (KPIs) tie a workload's behavior to the business outcomes it produces. Derive each KPI from a business outcome or priority, then analyze it against its target and adjust as the workload and business change.

Use dashboards to give operators and stakeholders a shared, real-time view of system and business health. Dashboards complement alerts: alerts tell you when something breaks, and dashboards show you what is happening and why.

Metrics such as latency, error rate, and capacity show how a system behaves. Regular review of those metrics against expectations and business outcomes helps you make decisions: what to tune, what to investigate, and what is already working.

Logs are the most detailed telemetry a workload produces, recording every request, error, and component decision. At production volume, no human being is reading logs line by line. Regular log analysis uses queries and machine assistance to extract patterns and answers from that detail.

A trace shows the path a request takes through your workload. Trace analysis looks at these paths at the scale of your entire architecture. While metrics quantify changes and logs record what each component did, traces show how the parts of your workload behaved together: which service added latency, which dependency returned an error, and which interaction pattern is drifting.

AI assistants now work at every stage of observability: they can instrument an application, write the queries, build the dashboards, recommend the objectives and alarms, and investigate what those alarms catch. Use them where they work the best. For example, an assistant analyzes large volumes of telemetry and correlates information across signals faster than a human can.

questions.title: How do you adopt change flow processes with quality gates?
questions.description: With AWS, you can define and manage your entire workload (applications, infrastructure, policy, governance, and operations) as code. This means you can apply the same engineering discipline that you use for application code to every element of your stack.

choices.title: Adopt a configuration, build, and release pipeline

helpfulResource.displayText: Manual builds and hand-applied configuration changes drift over time and create non-reproducible environments. A pipeline that combines version control, configuration management, and automated release removes that drift by making every change tracked, tested, and repeatable. When the pipeline is shared infrastructure owned centrally, workload teams inherit it and ship changes safely without rebuilding the same tooling.

improvementPlan.displayText: Adopt a configuration, build, and release pipeline

choices.title: Test and validate any and all changes

helpfulResource.displayText: Test every change before it reaches production, including application code, infrastructure, configuration, security controls, and operational procedures. When you run tests immediately after each change, defects are cheap to fix and developers get fast feedback.

improvementPlan.displayText: Test and validate any and all changes

choices.title: Implement practices to improve code quality

helpfulResource.displayText: Defects are cheapest to remove before a change is deployed. Practices such as test-driven development, code reviews, pair programming, and shared coding standards raise quality at the source, so fewer defects reach testing and production. A second reviewer catches errors, security flaws, and standards violations the author cannot see, and spreads knowledge across the team.

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement practices to improve code quality

helpfulResource.displayText: Manual steps in integration and deployment are where errors and delay accumulate. A developer who logs into a console to promote a change, or waits for a scheduled release window, adds risk and lead time. Full automation of the path from code commit through build, test, deployment, and validation removes those steps, so changes flow to production consistently.

Patching keeps systems secure, supported, and current with features, but patching manually does not scale and is error-prone. Treat patch management as a designed process: decide what to patch, when, and how it moves across environments, and then automate the mechanics. Rebuild systems from a known good image where you can, and use controlled in-place patching where you cannot.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you mitigate deployment risks?
questions.description: The design of your workload should include how it will be deployed, updated, and operated. Implement engineering practices that align with defect reduction and quick and safe fixes.

choices.title: Employ and test safe deployment strategies

helpfulResource.displayText: Safe deployment practices control how a change reaches customers, so that a defect affects the fewest of them before you catch it. When you release changes in increments and check health at each step, you limit the scope of impact and shorten recovery time.

improvementPlan.displayText: Employ and test safe deployment strategies

helpfulResource.displayText: Automated tests verify changes during deployment, and automated rollback reverses a change when predefined conditions signal failure. Together they shorten recovery time by removing manual delay.

choices.title: Develop and test rollout for consuming external dependencies

helpfulResource.displayText: Workloads often depend on external software, from security agents to third-party libraries. Updates to these dependencies can be as disruptive as your own changes, yet they often arrive on the vendor's schedule and bypass your normal controls. Treat external updates as changes you own. Test them, roll them out gradually, and maintain the ability to rollback, so you stay current on security fixes without accepting an unvalidated change straight into production.

improvementPlan.displayText: Develop and test rollout for consuming external dependencies

questions.title: How do you establish workload supportability for production?
questions.description: You should use a consistent process (including manual or automated checklists) to know when you are ready to go live with your workload or a change. This also helps you find any areas that you need to make plans to address. Create runbooks that document your routine activities and playbooks that guide your processes for issue resolution. Use a mechanism to manage changes that supports the delivery of business value and helps mitigate risks associated with change.

choices.title: Develop and test runbooks to perform procedures

helpfulResource.displayText: A runbook is a documented procedure that produces the same outcome every time, no matter who runs it. Teams use runbooks for routine and high-stakes work, from onboarding an engineer to deploying a release or recovering from an incident. Without them, operations depend on memory and habit, which produces inconsistent results and more errors.

improvementPlan.displayText: Develop and test runbooks to perform procedures

choices.title: Develop and test playbooks to respond to incidents

helpfulResource.displayText: A playbook is a step-by-step guide for investigating an incident from symptoms to root cause. You use playbooks to scope impact and diagnose problems consistently, whether a deployment failed or a service is degraded. Without them, investigation depends on individual recall and trial and error, which slows response and produces uneven results.

improvementPlan.displayText: Develop and test playbooks to respond to incidents

choices.title: Create support plans for production workloads

helpfulResource.displayText: Production workloads depend on software and services that your team does not operate. When one of those dependencies fails, your ability to respond depends on the support agreement you arranged in advance. A support plan defines the response you can expect, how to reach the vendor, and how to escalate during an incident.

improvementPlan.displayText: Create support plans for production workloads

helpfulResource.displayText: An operational readiness review (ORR) is a structured check that your team can operate a workload safely before it goes live and as it evolves. It uses a checklist built from best practices and past incidents to surface gaps while they are still cheap to fix.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you create an effective event response?
questions.description: With AWS, you can improve recovery time by replacing failed components with known good versions, rather than trying to repair them. You can then carry out a separate analysis on the failed resources.

helpfulResource.displayText: When each alert maps to a defined response, operators know what to do when it fires, and important signals aren't lost in low-value noise.

Manual handling of routine operational events is slow, inconsistent, and hard to scale. Automate the response to well-understood events to act immediately, apply the same remediation every time, and free operators for problems that need judgment.

When an incident exceeds what the first responder can resolve, someone must decide who acts next and with what authority. Escalation paths define when to escalate, who to involve at each level, and which actions are pre-approved, so decisions happen fast and the right people engage.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you learn and evolve from events?
questions.description: Include feedback loops within your procedures to rapidly identify areas for improvement and capture learnings from running operations. Keep what you learn in a searchable knowledge repository with clear ownership and a review cadence, so lessons stay findable and current instead of living in individual memory. Where a documented procedure diverges from what people actually do, treat the document as the defect and route the correction back to the runbook or playbook it belongs to. Share lessons learned across teams so the benefit is not confined to the team that earned it. Analyze trends within lessons learned and perform cross-team retrospective analysis of operations metrics to identify opportunities and methods for improvement. Implement changes intended to bring about improvement and evaluate the results to determine success.

helpfulResource.displayText: A structured post-incident analysis examines the contributing factors behind a customer-impacting event and converts those findings into changes that reduce the chance of recurrence.
With clear drivers for improvement, you evaluate opportunities against business outcomes and data, rank them by their effect, and automate work where the return justifies the effort.

Teams lose time and repeat mistakes when the knowledge they need is scattered or out of date. Knowledge management gives your organization a single, searchable place for cross-organization knowledge and a process to keep that information current. When people find accurate information quickly, they make better decisions, onboard faster, and depend less on individual memory.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you securely operate your workload?
questions.description: This capability covers establishing that foundation: separating workloads, defining and validating control objectives, reducing the security surface a team has to manage, automating the controls every workload inherits, modeling threats, and keeping current with new threats and capabilities. It does not cover the specific identity, network, data protection, or detection controls that the later capabilities address.

helpfulResource.displayText: An account is the strongest isolation boundary available to you. When you group unrelated workloads in a single account, a mistake or unauthorized access in one workload can reach the others. Separating workloads by environment and business criticality limits how far that reach extends, clarifies ownership, and makes cost and access boundaries explicit.

Control objectives translate compliance obligations and identified risks into outcomes your controls must achieve. Validate the controls at a point in time and over a period to produce evidence you can act on and report.

choices.title: Stay up to date with security threats and recommendations

helpfulResource.displayText: Monitor trusted threat intelligence to keep pace with new vulnerabilities and attack techniques. Where possible, adopt services that fold new intelligence in automatically so detection improves without constant manual effort.

improvementPlan.displayText: Stay up to date with security threats and recommendations

helpfulResource.displayText: Every control you operate yourself is a control you must configure, patch, monitor, and prove. Managed services shift some of that operational work to the provider, which reduces the surface you maintain and the compliance scope you own. Choosing where to hand off management is a deliberate trade-off between control, effort, and total cost of ownership.

choices.title: Automate deployment of standard security controls

helpfulResource.displayText: Manually-applied security controls can drift, vary between environments, and are hard to audit. Define controls as code, version them, test them, and deploy them through a pipeline to keep them consistent, reviewable, and repeatable.

improvementPlan.displayText: Automate deployment of standard security controls

choices.title: Identify threats and prioritize mitigations using a threat model

helpfulResource.displayText: A threat model is a structured way to find what can go wrong in a system and decide what to do about it before an unauthorized user does. Complex systems can obscure issues, and manual reviews might sometimes miss these threats. Model threats early in design, when fixes are cheap.

improvementPlan.displayText: Identify threats and prioritize mitigations using a threat model

choices.title: Evaluate and implement new security services and features regularly

helpfulResource.displayText: Cloud providers release new security capabilities continually. If you do not track them, your controls fall behind. Implement a repeatable way to learn about, evaluate, and adopt new features to keep your security posture current as the environment and threats evolve.

improvementPlan.displayText: Evaluate and implement new security services and features regularly

questions.title: How do you manage identities for people and machines?
questions.description: This capability covers identifying principals and their use cases, centralizing authentication, using short-lived credentials, storing the remaining secrets securely, and auditing and rotating what is left. It does not cover the permissions those identities are granted or how access to specific resources is authorized, which the permissions capability addresses.

helpfulResource.displayText: Every workload authenticates people, services, and devices, each with different risks and access needs. Before you choose authentication methods or providers, identify who and what interacts with your workload and what each interaction requires. This inventory shapes an identity design that scales as users and services grow.

Long-term credentials persist until someone removes them, which gives an unauthorized party durable access if the credentials are inadvertently disclosed. Temporary credentials expire automatically, which shrinks the window in which exposed credentials are useful. Use short-lived credentials for both human and machine access wherever a workload supports them, and reserve long-term credentials for the few cases that cannot avoid them.

Workloads prove their identity to databases, APIs, and third-party services with secrets such as passwords, API keys, and tokens. A secret in source code, a configuration file, or an environment variable is easy to disclose and hard to rotate. A secrets service encrypts these credentials, controls access, and rotates them automatically.

choices.title: Rely on a centralized identity provider for users and machines

helpfulResource.displayText: When each application manages its own identities, users juggle multiple logins and security teams lose a single view of who has access. A centralized identity provider makes one system the source of truth for authentication, authorization, and lifecycle management across your workloads. This applies to machine identities as well as people, so service-to-service calls authenticate through the same governed system.

improvementPlan.displayText: Rely on a centralized identity provider for users and machines

helpfulResource.displayText: Some credentials cannot be made temporary, and every long-term credential is a standing risk. The longer it lives, the more chances it has to be inadvertently disclosed, and the longer that disclosure stays useful. Regular auditing confirms that the right controls are in place, and regular rotation caps how long any single credential is valid.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you manage permissions for people and machines?
questions.description: This capability covers scoping permissions to function, managing authorization consistently across a workload, and controlling how resources are shared publicly, across accounts, and with third parties. It does not cover establishing the identities themselves, which the identity management capability addresses.

choices.title: Grant least privilege access in workload components

helpfulResource.displayText: Every component in a workload runs with some set of permissions. When those permissions exceed what a component needs, each component becomes a wider path for an unauthorized user to move through. Grant each component only the permissions its function requires, and remove access as functions change. This limits the impact of any single component under unauthorized control to what that component could already do.

improvementPlan.displayText: Grant least privilege access in workload components

choices.title: Use scalable and centralized permissions management in your workload

helpfulResource.displayText: When you have a workload with rich authorization needs, you must decide who can access and modify resources, often under changing conditions. When that logic lives inside application code or a custom database table, it drifts out of sync across components and becomes hard to audit or change. Manage permissions through a centralized, policy-based authorization service instead, so decisions stay consistent and reviewable as the workload grows.

improvementPlan.displayText: Use scalable and centralized permissions management in your workload

helpfulResource.displayText: Some resources need to be reachable from outside their own account, whether publicly or by another account, to support shared data or common tools. Such access tends to persist beyond the reason it was granted. Keep an inventory of which resources are shared and with whom, monitor it continuously, and reduce public and cross-account access to only the resources that require it. Apply the same scrutiny to internal access to sensitive resources, and verify which principals in your organization can reach them so access stays limited to those you intend.

choices.title: Share resources securely within your organization

helpfulResource.displayText: You often need the same resource in several accounts, or you need one account to reach a resource owned by another. Recreating a resource in every account or sharing the resource broadly are both imperfect solutions. Instead, share resources through controlled mechanisms with trusted entities only, and monitor those shares to limit access to what each consumer needs.

improvementPlan.displayText: Share resources securely within your organization

choices.title: Share resources securely with a third party

helpfulResource.displayText: A workload often depends on third-party tools that need access to your account, such as a monitoring or analytics service. Grant third parties least privilege access through temporary credentials, and work with the provider to keep the scope of impact small.

improvementPlan.displayText: Share resources securely with a third party

helpfulResource.displayText: Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you detect and investigate security events?
questions.description: Raw events on their own do not tell a team when to act. Metrics measured against a known baseline, alarms that reach the right responders, and dashboards tuned to each workload convert stored data into early warning. This capability covers building that visibility and acting on it. It does not cover the incident response process itself, which later capabilities address.

helpfulResource.displayText: Capture access logs, network flow records, and configuration change events from every component in your workload. This evidence helps you detect threats and reconstruct incidents.

Metrics, alarms, and dashboards turn security data into signals your team can act on. When you track the right measurements and present them clearly, you can spot early warning signs, respond before an incident escalates, and show whether your security posture is improving over time.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you protect your network resources?
questions.description: Effective network protection treats the network as a set of boundaries rather than a single perimeter. Components are grouped by their function, the sensitivity of the data they handle, and how they behave, and controls are placed at each boundary so only authorized flows pass. Traffic is inspected against expected patterns, and protections tighten as traffic moves closer to sensitive data. Because these controls span many accounts and change over time, they are most reliable when they are expressed as code and deployed through automation rather than configured manually.

helpfulResource.displayText: Group your workload components into network layers based on their data sensitivity and access needs. Separate components that must accept traffic from the internet, such as public web endpoints, from those that only communicate internally, such as databases. This grouping creates boundaries where you place controls to restrict the paths an unauthorized user can take toward sensitive systems.

choices.title: Control traffic flow within your network layers

helpfulResource.displayText: Within each network layer, segment traffic so that you permit only the flows required by your workload. Start with traffic between your environment and the internet or other external systems, then control the flows between internal components. Apply least privilege to network paths to limit how far an incident can spread.

improvementPlan.displayText: Control traffic flow within your network layers

helpfulResource.displayText: Inspect traffic between your network layers to confirm it matches expected patterns. Analyze flows, metadata, and behavior to detect and respond to events. Make protections stricter as traffic moves closer to sensitive data.

Automate deployment of network protections with infrastructure as code and continuous integration and delivery pipelines. With automation, you can version network changes, deploy them faster, detect drift from intended configuration, and make protections repeatable across teams and accounts.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you protect your compute resources?
questions.description: This capability covers building compute from a known secure baseline, verifying the integrity and provenance of software before it runs, finding and remediating vulnerabilities by workload risk, reducing manual management and interactive access, and automating these protections so they hold at scale. It does not cover the network, identity, or data protection controls that other capabilities address.

helpfulResource.displayText: Software accumulates known vulnerabilities as researchers find flaws in operating systems, libraries, and dependencies. Vulnerability management is the ongoing practice of finding these weaknesses, judging their risk to your workload, and remediating them before they can be used for unauthorized access. Prioritize fixes by data sensitivity and the business impact of the affected component.

A hardened image is a base operating system, container, or dependency set stripped to only what the workload needs and configured to a known secure standard. Provisioning compute from hardened images reduces the available vectors for unauthorized use and limits the impact if unintended access occurs. Acquire runtime dependencies only from trusted sources, verify their signatures, and store approved versions where your build and deploy processes can reference them.

choices.title: Reduce manual management and interactive access

helpfulResource.displayText: Interactive login is the traditional way to configure, patch, and troubleshoot a server. A listening remote-access service is a path an unauthorized user can target, and manual steps invite human error and shared credentials. Capturing management actions as automation, and reserving direct access for emergencies, reduces the attack surface and the chance of an unintended change.

improvementPlan.displayText: Reduce manual management and interactive access

helpfulResource.displayText: Software artifacts can be altered between when a vendor publishes them and when your workload runs them. Use cryptographic signatures to confirm an artifact was not altered and came from its claimed source. Sign your own code and images so your compute environments run only what you approved.

Manual security operations do not keep pace with the rate at which compute resources change and vulnerabilities appear. Automating scanning, patching, verification, and remediation reduces the chance of a misconfiguration reaching production and shortens the time from detection to remediation.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you classify your data?
questions.description: This capability covers naming sensitivity levels and recording where sensitive data resides, sizing controls to each level, automating identification as data grows and moves, and managing data through its lifecycle from ingestion to destruction. It does not cover the specific encryption and access controls for data at rest or in transit, which later capabilities address.

helpfulResource.displayText: A data classification scheme names the sensitivity levels in your organization, the handling rules for each, and who owns the decision. To apply the right controls, know the classification, location, and legal and compliance obligations of the data your workload processes.

choices.title: Apply data protection controls based on data sensitivity

helpfulResource.displayText: Not all data needs the same protection. Applying controls that match each sensitivity level guards your most sensitive data from unauthorized access while keeping lower-sensitivity data available.

improvementPlan.displayText: Apply data protection controls based on data sensitivity

helpfulResource.displayText: Automating identification and classification finds sensitive data, confirms that the right controls apply, and flags data stored or handled in unauthorized ways. Apply it before data reaches production and continually in running environments.

Lifecycle management defines how data is handled when it arrives, how it is transformed, how long it is kept, and how it is destroyed. Tie these rules to your classification levels to keep protection appropriate as data ages and make retention and destruction deliberate.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you protect your data at rest?
questions.description: Encryption protects data only as well as its keys are protected, so managing keys across their lifecycle is central to this capability. That lifecycle covers generation, storage, access, rotation, and monitoring. Auditing how keys are used confirms that access controls hold and surfaces anomalous behavior, and making protection the default state keeps it from depending on anyone remembering to turn it on.

helpfulResource.displayText: Secure key management covers how you generate, store, control access to, rotate, and monitor key material across its lifecycle. Treat keys as the most sensitive asset in your workload

Encrypting data at rest keeps it confidential even when the storage layer is exposed. Because storage is easy to create and misconfigure, make encryption the default for new resources and keep an inventory of any unencrypted data.

Manual data protection controls drift out of compliance as storage grows and changes. Automation enforces those controls continuously, catches misconfigurations before deployment, and remediates drift at runtime. It also creates the backups and detective coverage that protect data through operational failures and security events.

Encryption protects data at rest, and access control decides who can reach that data. Apply least privilege, isolate data by sensitivity, block public access, and preserve prior versions to limit unauthorized access and damage from accidental or unauthorized changes.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you protect your data in transit?
questions.description: This capability covers establishing that protection: managing certificates and private keys across their lifecycle, enforcing encryption on traffic entering, leaving, and moving within the environment, and authenticating the parties to a communication. It does not cover protecting data once it is stored, which the data-at-rest capability addresses.

choices.title: Implement secure key and certificate management

helpfulResource.displayText: Digital certificates and their private keys establish trust in network communications and prove the identity of services, devices, and users. Proper certificate management means that you provision, distribute, renew, and revoke certificates without exposing private key material or letting certificates lapse. Automate these tasks, as manual certificate handling can cause security incidents.

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement secure key and certificate management

helpfulResource.displayText: Encryption in transit protects data as it moves between systems and across networks you do not control. Enforcing it means requiring secure protocols for sensitive traffic, rejecting weak or outdated ones, and confirming that both endpoints negotiate strong parameters. Your organization's policies, regulatory obligations, and standards define what counts as strong for your workloads.

Authenticating network communications means each party verifies the other's identity before they exchange data, using protocols that support authentication. An attacker with unauthorized network access can move laterally and send requests that appear internal, so network location alone is insufficient evidence of identity. Apply it to internal service-to-service traffic as well as traffic from external users.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you anticipate, respond to, and recover from security incidents?
questions.description: This capability covers identifying responders, developing and testing incident management plans and playbooks, running simulations, and learning from incidents. The emergency access, security tooling, and forensic capabilities it relies on are established as foundational capabilities rather than rebuilt for each workload.

choices.title: Identify key personnel and external resources

helpfulResource.displayText: Before an incident occurs, identify the internal responders, external partners, and legal contacts who investigate, communicate, and make decisions during a security event. Keep the list current so you can reach the right people quickly when one occurs.

improvementPlan.displayText: Identify key personnel and external resources

helpfulResource.displayText: An incident management plan gives your team a known way to act when a security event occurs. It defines roles, communication paths, severity levels, and the phases of response, so decisions are made ahead of time. Build a plan that fits your workload and connects to your organization's broader response program.

choices.title: Develop and test security incident response playbooks

helpfulResource.displayText: A playbook gives a responder the technical steps to investigate and contain a scenario. A separate management plan defines who responds and how you communicate.

improvementPlan.displayText: Develop and test security incident response playbooks

helpfulResource.displayText: Simulations, sometimes called game days, put your team through realistic security scenarios so they practice their roles, tools, and communication before a real incident. Regular exercises reveal gaps in plans and playbooks while the stakes are low.

choices.title: Establish a framework for learning from incidents

helpfulResource.displayText: Use a structured review to close the gaps in tools and processes that let an incident happen. Focus on fixing systems and keep reviews blameless.

improvementPlan.displayText: Establish a framework for learning from incidents

helpfulResource.displayText: Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you incorporate and validate application security throughout the design, development, and deployment lifecycle?
questions.description: This capability covers embedding security throughout the software lifecycle: team ownership and skills, secure coding and code review, automated and manual testing, supply chain and dependency control, and secured programmatic deployment. It does not cover the identity, network, data protection, or detection controls that other capabilities address.

choices.title: Embed security ownership in workload teams, and train for application security

helpfulResource.displayText: Security decisions happen throughout development. When the teams that build software own its security, they catch risks during design. Give builders the authority and training to make well-informed, sound security decisions.

improvementPlan.displayText: Embed security ownership in workload teams, and train for application security

helpfulResource.displayText: Most software vulnerabilities come from a small set of recurring coding mistakes. Established secure coding standards capture how to avoid these mistakes so that each team does not have to rediscover them. Adopt a recognized standard, tailor it to your technology stack, and build it into how your teams write and review code.

choices.title: Automate testing throughout the development and release lifecycle

helpfulResource.displayText: Manual security checks run late and inconsistently, and they depend on a reviewer being available. Automated tests run the same way every time and give builders feedback while the code is still new. Automate security testing across the development and release lifecycle so issues appear early and known flaws do not reach production.

improvementPlan.displayText: Automate testing throughout the development and release lifecycle

helpfulResource.displayText: Automated scans and code reviews find known patterns but miss flaws that appear only when someone chains steps together or abuses business logic. Penetration testing places a skilled tester in the role of an unauthorized user to find those gaps and check whether your detective controls work. Run these tests on a regular schedule and after major changes.

In a code review, a team member other than the author reads the code delta to find defects, vulnerabilities, and departures from your standards. Reviews spread knowledge across the team and help less experienced developers learn. Automated tools handle mechanical checks so reviewers concentrate on logic and design.

choices.title: Centralize services for packages and dependencies

helpfulResource.displayText: Every third-party package brings its own vulnerabilities, sub-dependencies, and risk of disappearing or being tampered with. Route dependencies through a central, controlled source so you can scan them, approve them, and keep building when public repositories are unavailable.

improvementPlan.displayText: Centralize services for packages and dependencies

helpfulResource.displayText: Manual deployments introduce human error and make it hard to prove that what you tested is what you released. Programmatic deployment runs the same steps every time, removes people from the production path, and gives you a way to verify the integrity of each release. Externalize configuration so one artifact runs in any environment, and sign packages so you can prove they did not change.

choices.title: Regularly assess security properties of the pipelines

helpfulResource.displayText: A pipeline holds the permissions to build and deploy your software, which makes it a high-value target. Apply the same security principles to the pipeline that you apply to any workload, with particular attention to separating permissions. Reassess the pipeline's security properties on a schedule.

improvementPlan.displayText: Regularly assess security properties of the pipelines

questions.title: How do you manage service quotas and constraints?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization knows, monitors, and manages the quotas and constraints its workloads depend on: distinguishing adjustable quotas from fixed constraints, tracking usage across every account and Region, accommodating fixed quotas through architecture, automating quota management, and keeping enough headroom for a failover to succeed within the quotas that remain.

choices.title: Aware of service quotas and constraints

helpfulResource.displayText: Cloud services set quotas on how many resources you can provision and how fast you can call operations. Some quotas you can raise on request. Others are fixed by the resource itself and cannot change. To plan capacity, track which quotas apply to your workload and how close your usage runs to each quota.

improvementPlan.displayText: Aware of service quotas and constraints

choices.title: Manage service quotas across accounts and regions

helpfulResource.displayText: Workloads that span multiple accounts or Regions carry a separate set of quota values in each space. A resilience design that fails over to a secondary location depends on that location holding enough quota to absorb the shifted load. Request and reconcile quotas in every environment where production traffic runs or could run after a failover.

improvementPlan.displayText: Manage service quotas across accounts and regions

choices.title: Accommodate fixed service quotas and constraints through architecture

helpfulResource.displayText: When a design assumes it can grow past a fixed quota or physical resource constraint, it fails at scale with no remediation path. Design around fixed quotas from the start so the workload performs under both normal and peak conditions.

improvementPlan.displayText: Accommodate fixed service quotas and constraints through architecture

helpfulResource.displayText: Quota usage changes as a workload grows, and an increase request takes time to approve. Monitor consumption against each quota and raise quotas ahead of demand to support planned growth. Without monitoring, the first sign that you have run out of headroom is a failed operation in production.

Manual quota tracking drifts out of date as a workload grows and spreads across accounts and Regions. Automate the monitoring of usage against quotas, and consider automating the increase requests. Automation keeps quota values aligned with real demand and removes the human delay between noticing a quota and acting on it.

choices.title: Verify that a sufficient gap exists between the current quotas and the maximum usage to accommodate failover

helpfulResource.displayText: A failover creates new resources before the old ones stop counting against your quota. If the quota has no room for that overlap, the replacement cannot start and the recovery fails. Keep a deliberate gap between your quota and your normal usage so a zonal, network, or Regional failover fits within the quota.

improvementPlan.displayText: Verify that a sufficient gap exists between the current quotas and the maximum usage to accommodate failover

questions.title: How do you plan your network topology?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization plans a network topology for reliability: building highly available connectivity to public endpoints, provisioning redundant paths between private networks in the cloud and on premises, and planning addressing and structure in anticipation of failure and future growth. Plan the topology so that the loss of a single component, path, or location does not sever the connection between users and the workload, or between the workload and the systems it depends on.

choices.title: Use highly available network connectivity for your workload public endpoints

helpfulResource.displayText: Users reach your workload through its public endpoints. If the network path fails, users can't reach the workload even when it is healthy and running. Highly available connectivity spreads that path across redundant components for name resolution, content delivery, load balancing, and traffic routing. If one component fails, users still reach the workload.

improvementPlan.displayText: Use highly available network connectivity for your workload public endpoints

choices.title: Provision redundant connectivity between private networks in the cloud and on-premises environments

helpfulResource.displayText: Workloads in the cloud often depend on systems that stay in a corporate data center or private network. A single connection between the two environments is a single point of failure: if it drops, the dependent services stop communicating. Redundant connectivity uses two or more independent links and traffic paths, so the failure of one link does not sever the connection between environments.

improvementPlan.displayText: Provision redundant connectivity between private networks in the cloud and on-premises environments

helpfulResource.displayText: Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you design your workload service architecture?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization designs the service architecture of a workload for reliability: choosing a segmentation level deliberately, drawing service boundaries along business domains, and defining machine-readable contracts between services. Together these decisions let components scale, recover, and release on their own, and they contain a failure within one part of the workload rather than letting it spread across the whole.

choices.title: Choose how to segment your workload

helpfulResource.displayText: How you divide a workload (segmentation) sets the boundaries for where teams work and where faults are contained. Finer-grained segments improve agility and limit the blast radius of a failure, but they add the complexity of a distributed system. The right level depends on your reliability requirements, your team structure, and how much operational overhead you can absorb.

improvementPlan.displayText: Choose how to segment your workload

choices.title: Build services focused on specific business domains and functionality

helpfulResource.displayText: Where you draw service boundaries decides how independently your teams and services can operate. Boundaries that follow business domains provide ownership to each team of a coherent slice of functionality so that they can set their own reliability requirements. Boundaries drawn along technical layers, such as user interface or database, force many teams to coordinate on a single change. Aligning services to business capabilities keeps failures and updates contained within one domain.

improvementPlan.displayText: Build services focused on specific business domains and functionality

helpfulResource.displayText: A service contract is a documented, machine-readable agreement between an API producer and its consumers. It defines the operations, data types, and fields that both sides rely on, so each can change its implementation without breaking the other. With a versioning strategy, consumers keep using the current API and migrate on their own schedule. Producers deploy whenever they are ready, and teams pick the technology stack that suits them.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you design interactions in a distributed system to prevent failures?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization designs the interactions between the components of a distributed system to prevent failures: classifying each dependency by its communication style, decoupling components through published interfaces and durable intermediaries, designing control systems to perform a constant amount of work, and making mutating operations idempotent so retries and duplicate delivery do not corrupt state.

choices.title: Identify the kind of distributed systems you depend on

helpfulResource.displayText: Distributed systems communicate in one of three styles: synchronous, asynchronous, or batch. Each style carries different failure characteristics, latency behavior, and coupling. When you know which style each dependency uses, you can choose error handling, timeouts, and retry strategies that match how that dependency behaves. Misidentifying the style leads to brittle chains, indefinite waits, and duplicate processing.

improvementPlan.displayText: Identify the kind of distributed systems you depend on

helpfulResource.displayText: Loose coupling isolates the behavior of one component from the components that depend on it. When a component changes or fails, that isolation limits the impact to a single boundary. Dependent components interact through a published, versioned interface or a durable intermediary, so each side can change and scale independently.

Systems can fail when load changes suddenly and by a large amount. A constant-work design performs the same amount of work regardless of conditions. A surge in failures or demand does not create a matching surge in the system's work. Because the system behaves the same in normal and failure modes, large and rapid changes do not threaten its stability.

An idempotent operation produces the same result whether it runs once or many times, so a client can safely retry a request. Retries and duplicate delivery are normal in distributed systems, and idempotency makes these operations safer and more consistent.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you design interactions in a distributed system to mitigate or withstand failures?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization designs the interactions between distributed components to withstand and recover from failure: degrading gracefully when a dependency is unhealthy, throttling requests to protect capacity, controlling retries and timeouts so clients do not deepen an impairment, failing fast and managing queue backlogs, removing local state so nodes stay interchangeable, and preparing emergency levers that shed non-critical load during an incident. The result is a lower mean time to recovery and a higher mean time between failures.

choices.title: Implement graceful degradation to transform applicable hard dependencies into soft dependencies

helpfulResource.displayText: A component with a hard dependency fails when the dependency fails. Graceful degradation converts hard dependencies into soft dependencies, so a component continues to deliver its core function even when a dependency is unhealthy. The component might return stale data, alternate data, or a reduced response, but it does not fail outright.

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement graceful degradation to transform applicable hard dependencies into soft dependencies

helpfulResource.displayText: Your workload can only process so many requests before it runs out of resources. Throttling protects that capacity by accepting requests up to a defined rate and rejecting the excess with a response that signals the request was throttled. This keeps your workload processing its supported volume during traffic spikes, flooding attacks, and retry storms instead of collapsing under load.

Retries recover from transient failures, but uncontrolled retries turn a small impairment into a large one. Retry requests at progressively longer intervals using exponential backoff, randomize those intervals with jitter, and cap the total number of attempts. Controlled retries release resources and give a struggling system time to recover.

When a service cannot respond successfully, failing fast releases the resources tied to the request and lets a strained service recover. When a service can normally succeed but falls behind during spikes, a queue buffers requests so clients can move on. Both patterns improve reliability, but only when queue backlogs are managed so the service does not process stale requests.

A call with no timeout can wait forever and hold resources while a dependency is impaired. Set both connection and request timeouts on every call across a process boundary, verify them, and do not rely on framework defaults. Framework defaults do not reflect your workload and are often infinite or far higher than your service goals allow.

A stateless component keeps no client-specific data on local disk or in memory between requests. Any compute node can serve any request, so you can replace or scale nodes without an availability impact. Offloading session and user data to a shared store makes horizontal scaling and node-level fault tolerance possible.

An emergency lever is a rapid, pre-tested process that reduces availability impact during an incident. It disables, throttles, or changes the behavior of a component or dependency, so you can shed a non-critical failure or absorb an unexpected demand spike. Your workload keeps performing its business-critical functions while the lever is active.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you monitor workload resources?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization monitors the resources a workload depends on across four phases: generating telemetry from every component, aggregating it into metrics you can reason about, processing it in real time to notify responders and invoke automated recovery, and storing it for analysis over time. It also covers reviewing the monitoring strategy as the workload changes, and tracing requests end to end so you can find where errors and latency originate in a distributed system.

choices.title: Monitor all components for the workload (Generation)

helpfulResource.displayText: Collect telemetry from each tier so you can detect degradation early and confirm that the workload delivers its intended business outcomes. Without broad instrumentation, failures surface first as customer complaints.

improvementPlan.displayText: Monitor all components for the workload (Generation)

helpfulResource.displayText: Raw telemetry from individual components rarely answers the questions that matter during an incident. Aggregation turns scattered logs and metrics into a coherent view of how the workload behaves. When you calculate metrics that span components and enrich them with context, you can detect anomalies, correlate failures, and find the cause of a problem faster.

choices.title: Send notifications with real-time processing and alarming

helpfulResource.displayText: Real-time notifications alert responders and trigger automation the moment a metric crosses a threshold or a significant event occurs. The design challenge is setting thresholds that catch real problems without burying responders in noise.

improvementPlan.displayText: Send notifications with real-time processing and alarming

helpfulResource.displayText: Manual response to alarms introduces delay and the chance of human error. When you automate the response to a detected event, systems take corrective action in seconds and apply the same procedure every time. Automated responses range from healing a single failed component to redirecting traffic across Availability Zones or Regions.

Analyzing accumulated log data reveals trends, recurring failure patterns, and slow regressions that no single alarm exposes. This analysis also requires a data-management strategy that retains logs long enough to be useful and controls storage cost.

choices.title: Regularly review monitoring scope and metrics

helpfulResource.displayText: Monitoring drifts out of date as a workload and its architecture change. Review your monitoring on a regular cadence, and after significant events or changes, so it keeps pace with how the workload behaves.

improvementPlan.displayText: Regularly review monitoring scope and metrics

choices.title: Monitor end-to-end tracing of requests through your system

helpfulResource.displayText: In a distributed system, a single request touches many components, and a failure or slowdown in any one of them affects the whole. Tracing follows each request across those components so you can pinpoint where errors and latency originate. This shortens root-cause discovery and reduces the mean time to resolve incidents.

improvementPlan.displayText: Monitor end-to-end tracing of requests through your system

questions.title: How do you design your workload to adapt to changes in demand?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization designs a workload to match resources to demand: provisioning and scaling through automation rather than manually, recovering capacity when a component becomes impaired, adding resources as healthy demand grows, and validating the whole arrangement with load tests that find the breaking point before customers do.

choices.title: Use automation when obtaining or scaling resources

helpfulResource.displayText: Manual provisioning produces environments that drift apart and fail in non-reproducible ways. When you define resources as code and automate provisioning and scaling, every environment is built the same way and every change is reviewable. This turns capacity into a property of your architecture.

improvementPlan.displayText: Use automation when obtaining or scaling resources

choices.title: Obtain resources upon detection of impairment to a workload

helpfulResource.displayText: Adding or replacing unhealthy resources automatically can restore service before your customers feel the impact. This requires quick detection and a defined response. Reactive scaling is a recovery mechanism, distinct from scaling that anticipates rising demand.

improvementPlan.displayText: Obtain resources upon detection of impairment to a workload

choices.title: Obtain resources upon detection that more resources are needed for a workload

helpfulResource.displayText: Provisioning enough capacity in advance to cover peak demand wastes money during quiet periods and still risks running short when a peak exceeds the estimate. Provisioning capacity as demand appears removes both problems, but only if the workload can add resources fast enough and the scaling signal reflects real demand.

improvementPlan.displayText: Obtain resources upon detection that more resources are needed for a workload

helpfulResource.displayText: A load test drives representative traffic at a workload until something breaks, which reveals where capacity runs out and which metric warns you first. Without this evidence, you discover your limits during a real peak.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you implement change?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization implements change safely: documenting standard activities as version-controlled runbooks, gating releases on automated functional and resilience tests, replacing infrastructure from code rather than editing it in place, and running deployments and patching through automation with tested rollback.

choices.title: Use runbooks for standard activities such as deployment

helpfulResource.displayText: A runbook is a documented procedure that produces a specific, predictable outcome for a routine operation. Runbooks make standard activities such as deployments, patching, and DNS changes repeatable across people and teams. When a procedure is written down and validated, the result no longer depends on who runs it or whether they remember every step.

improvementPlan.displayText: Use runbooks for standard activities such as deployment

choices.title: Integrate functional testing as part of your deployment

helpfulResource.displayText: Functional tests confirm that code behaves as the requirements specify before it reaches customers. When these tests run automatically inside the deployment pipeline and a failure stops the release, defects are caught in a controlled environment before they reach production.

improvementPlan.displayText: Integrate functional testing as part of your deployment

choices.title: Integrate resilience testing as part of your deployment

helpfulResource.displayText: Resilience testing introduces failures to measure how a system behaves under disruption and to expose unanticipated weaknesses. Running these tests as part of deployment builds evidence that the system can withstand and recover from real-world failures.

improvementPlan.displayText: Integrate resilience testing as part of your deployment

helpfulResource.displayText: Immutable infrastructure is a model in which running resources are never modified in place. For each change, build new infrastructure with the change, deploy it alongside the existing resources, and shift traffic after you validate the new set. This approach removes failures caused by undocumented, in-place modifications that leave environments in unknown states.

Changes to production are one of the largest sources of operational risk. Automate deployments and patching to remove manual steps where human error exists so that every change follows the same tested path.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you back up data?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization protects the data its workloads depend on: identifying and classifying each source, deciding whether to back it up or reproduce it, running backups automatically to meet recovery point and recovery time objectives, securing and encrypting the copies, keeping critical copies immutable and isolated from production, and testing recovery on a schedule so a backup is a verified capability rather than an assumption.

choices.title: Identify and back up all data that needs to be backed up, or reproduce the data from sources

helpfulResource.displayText: Not all data is equally valuable, and you can recreate some from an authoritative source rather than back it up. Decide what to protect, how often, and by which method to build a recovery strategy that meets your tolerance for loss.

improvementPlan.displayText: Identify and back up all data that needs to be backed up, or reproduce the data from sources

helpfulResource.displayText: Backups often hold the same sensitive data as production, yet they receive less protection. Anyone who gains unauthorized access to your backups can read or destroy the one copy you rely on to recover. Protecting backups means controlling who can access them, detecting that access, and encrypting the data so an accidental exposure does not become a breach.

Manual backups fail in predictable ways. For example, people forget, schedules slip, and a missed backup goes unnoticed until someone needs to recover. Automating backups on a schedule tied to your tolerance for data loss removes the human step and produces a record of whether each backup succeeded.

choices.title: Perform periodic recovery of the data to verify backup integrity and processes

helpfulResource.displayText: Backups can be incomplete, corrupted, or slower to restore than your recovery targets allow, and you may only find out when you try to restore the backup. Regular recovery testing verifies you can restore a working system from backups within your recovery objectives.

improvementPlan.displayText: Perform periodic recovery of the data to verify backup integrity and processes

choices.title: Implement cyber resilience for backup data

helpfulResource.displayText: A ransomware or destructive event can breach the production environment or its identities and then delete or tamper with the backup copies you rely on to recover. Cyber resilience keeps backup data protected from deletion and tampering, so you can still recover even when production itself is affected.

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement cyber resilience for backup data

helpfulResource.displayText: Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you use fault isolation to protect your workload?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization uses fault isolation to keep a failure from spreading: deploying compute and data across multiple isolated locations, automating recovery for the components that cannot leave a single location, and partitioning a workload into independent cells so one fault reaches only a fraction of the requests.

choices.title: Deploy the workload to multiple locations

helpfulResource.displayText: Fires, floods, power loss, network faults, and human error can disable a data center or affect an entire geographic area. Distributing a workload's compute and data across multiple isolated locations removes this single point of failure, so the workload stays available when one location fails. The right number of locations depends on how much downtime and data loss the business can accept.

improvementPlan.displayText: Deploy the workload to multiple locations

choices.title: Automate recovery for components constrained to a single location

helpfulResource.displayText: Some components cannot run in more than one location. A licensing limit, a single-instance data store, or a legacy system may tie a component to one Availability Zone or one data center. When you cannot spread such a component across locations, resilience has to come from the ability to rebuild it quickly. Automating that rebuild keeps recovery within the time and data-loss limits the business has set.

improvementPlan.displayText: Automate recovery for components constrained to a single location

choices.title: Use bulkhead architectures to limit scope of impact

helpfulResource.displayText: A failure in a shared component can spread to every request a workload handles. Bulkhead architectures, also called cell-based architectures, divide a workload into independent instances that each serve a subset of requests. Because the instances share no state, a failure is confined to one of them, so most requests continue unaffected. This containment works even for faults that would otherwise be hard to isolate.

improvementPlan.displayText: Use bulkhead architectures to limit scope of impact

helpfulResource.displayText: Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you design your workload to withstand component failures?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization designs a workload to keep running when its components fail: detecting faults at every layer, failing over to healthy resources, automating recovery so it does not wait for a person, keeping recovery actions on the most available paths, holding capacity in advance for static stability, notifying teams even when automation resolves an event, and designing to the availability target the business set.

choices.title: Monitor all components of the workload to detect failures

helpfulResource.displayText: You cannot heal, fail over, or scale a component until you know it has failed. Monitor every layer of your workload continuously and measure both technical health and business outcomes. When detection is fast and complete, automated and human responses have time to limit customer impact.

improvementPlan.displayText: Monitor all components of the workload to detect failures

helpfulResource.displayText: When one resource fails, healthy resources keep serving requests. Distribute load across independent resources, Availability Zones, or Regions so that any single impairment removes only part of your capacity. Then add mechanisms to detect the impairment and shift traffic away from it, so a localized fault does not spread to the whole workload.

When a component fails, automated actions should remediate it. Some degradations heal through a service's own internal mechanisms, while others need a resource to be restarted, replaced, or removed. Automate healing on all layers to improve recovery time and reduce manual intervention.

choices.title: Rely on the data plane and not the control plane during recovery

helpfulResource.displayText: A control plane creates, changes, and describes resources, while a data plane carries the day-to-day traffic those resources serve. During a large impairment, when you most need recovery to work, control planes are more likely to be degraded and slower to respond. Design recovery to lean on data plane actions and to use as few control plane operations as possible.

improvementPlan.displayText: Rely on the data plane and not the control plane during recovery

choices.title: Use static stability to prevent bimodal behavior

helpfulResource.displayText: A statically stable workload behaves the same way whether or not a failure is occurring. Bimodal behavior is the opposite: the workload acts one way in normal operation and a different way during a failure, usually because it tries to acquire new resources at the moment of impairment. Design workloads to operate in a single mode so their behavior stays predictable when a component fails.

improvementPlan.displayText: Use static stability to prevent bimodal behavior

choices.title: Send notifications when events impact availability

helpfulResource.displayText: Send a notification whenever a threshold is breached, even when automation has already resolved the underlying event. Automated healing keeps a workload reliable, but it can also obscure recurring problems that need a real fix. Notify the right teams so they can spot patterns, including the failures that auto-healing absorbs, and address root causes before those failures grow.

improvementPlan.displayText: Send notifications when events impact availability

choices.title: Architect your product to meet availability targets and uptime service level agreements (SLAs)

helpfulResource.displayText: If you publish or privately commit to an availability target or uptime SLA, build your architecture and operations to support it from the start. Define the target during design, and let it drive the technology choices and trade-offs.

improvementPlan.displayText: Architect your product to meet availability targets and uptime service level agreements (SLAs)

questions.title: How do you test reliability?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization tests the reliability of its workloads: documenting investigation playbooks, learning from every incident through structured analysis, validating scaling and performance against measured targets, injecting controlled faults to expose unanticipated failure modes, and rehearsing failure response in regular game days. Run these tests often, because a workload changes and yesterday's evidence expires.

helpfulResource.displayText: A playbook guides responders through detecting, analyzing, containing, and resolving a failure scenario. Playbooks shorten the time to diagnose an incident and make investigations repeatable.

Post-incident analysis is the structured review of a customer-impacting event to find its contributing factors and prevent recurrence. Done well, it produces durable improvements across every workload that shares the same design, which helps you avoid repeating incidents.
Scalability and performance testing validates that your workload meets its throughput, latency, and scaling targets under realistic load before customers reach the limits.

Chaos engineering injects controlled faults into a system to verify that it withstands and recovers from real-world disruptions. Running these experiments regularly, in or close to production, builds confidence that recovery mechanisms work.

A game day is a scheduled exercise where your team responds to a simulated failure in a production-like environment, using the same people and procedures you would use for a real event. Practice events like this make incident response a routine activity.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you plan for disaster recovery (DR)?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization plans for disaster recovery across a workload's life: setting recovery objectives from business impact, choosing a recovery strategy that meets them at a cost the business accepts, testing failover under realistic conditions, keeping the recovery site in parity with the primary, and automating recovery so it runs reliably when an incident hits.

choices.title: Define recovery objectives for downtime and data loss

helpfulResource.displayText: Failures interrupt service and can leave data lost, stale, or inconsistent. Two objectives set the target for how fast you recover and how much data you can afford to lose: a recovery time objective (RTO) and a recovery point objective (RPO). Define both for every workload, based on business impact.

improvementPlan.displayText: Define recovery objectives for downtime and data loss

choices.title: Use defined recovery strategies to meet the recovery objectives

helpfulResource.displayText: A workload needs a planned way to run from a recovery site when its primary location cannot serve it. Choosing that plan is a trade-off between how fast you recover and how much standing infrastructure you pay for and operate. Define a strategy for each workload, drawn from a small set of reusable patterns.

improvementPlan.displayText: Use defined recovery strategies to meet the recovery objectives

choices.title: Test disaster recovery implementation to validate the implementation

helpfulResource.displayText: Assumptions about capacity, permissions, and timing go stale as a system evolves. Test failover regularly, under production conditions, to confirm that recovery works and that the team can perform it within the objectives you set.

improvementPlan.displayText: Test disaster recovery implementation to validate the implementation

choices.title: Manage configuration drift at the DR site or Region

helpfulResource.displayText: Over time, the primary and recovery sites diverge as changes land on the primary but not the recovery site. This drift is only exposed when a failover occurs. Keep infrastructure, configuration, and data in parity so recovery is complete and predictable.

improvementPlan.displayText: Manage configuration drift at the DR site or Region

helpfulResource.displayText: During an incident, manual steps invite mistakes and extend downtime. Automate recovery so it runs reliably and repeatably, observe it while it works, and maintain the ability to stop it if it goes wrong.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you validate and manage your workload's performance requirements?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization identifies, validates, and manages performance requirements: tracing them to business objectives, weighing performance against the other non-functional requirements, expressing adherence through measurable KPIs, and defining the degradation alerts and tolerances that signal when performance falls short.

choices.title: Validate requirements align to business needs

helpfulResource.displayText: Performance efficiency depends on knowing what the business needs from a workload. When requirements are vague or assumed, teams optimize the wrong things and spend effort where it returns little value. A structured process to identify, document, validate, and manage performance requirements keeps engineering work aligned with business outcomes and gives every stakeholder a shared definition of fast enough.

improvementPlan.displayText: Validate requirements align to business needs

choices.title: Evaluate the trade-offs between performance and other non-functional requirements

helpfulResource.displayText: Every performance improvement has a cost in another dimension: consistency, durability, cost, operational simplicity, or security. Weigh each trade-off against business priorities and record the reasoning.

improvementPlan.displayText: Evaluate the trade-offs between performance and other non-functional requirements

choices.title: Derive and establish KPIs that validate adherence to your performance requirements

helpfulResource.displayText: Key performance indicators turn raw operational metrics into business-relevant signals that show whether a workload meets its goals.

improvementPlan.displayText: Derive and establish KPIs that validate adherence to your performance requirements

choices.title: Establish criteria for performance degradation alerts and tolerances

helpfulResource.displayText: Performance degradation alerts and tolerance thresholds give teams early warning of problems so they can respond before users are affected. Define what counts as degradation, set how much deviation you tolerate, and route alerts to the people who can act.

improvementPlan.displayText: Establish criteria for performance degradation alerts and tolerances

helpfulResource.displayText: Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you select and use compute resources to meet performance requirements?
questions.description: This capability covers how an organization selects compute to fit the workload, measures how that compute performs, and keeps it matched to demand over time. It spans choosing the compute model and hardware for each component, collecting the metrics that show where resources work hard or sit idle, right-sizing and scaling to track real load, and offloading suitable work to specialized accelerators.

choices.title: Select the best compute options for your workload

helpfulResource.displayText: The compute model you choose determines a workload's performance, cost, and operational effort. Workloads differ in shape: some run constantly, some react to events, some process large batches. Matching the compute model to that shape lets a workload perform well without wasting capacity or operator time.

improvementPlan.displayText: Select the best compute options for your workload

helpfulResource.displayText: Compute metrics show how hard your resources work and where they stall. Collect them continuously to spot bottlenecks and idle capacity before they affect users or budgets. Right-sizing and scaling decisions depend on these metrics.

Right-sizing matches the type and amount of compute to what the workload uses. Provision too much and you pay for idle capacity. Provision too little and performance degrades and users feel it. Because demand and instance options change, revisit right-sizing regularly to improve performance and cost.

Dynamic scaling adjusts compute up and down automatically as load changes, so you hold performance during peaks without paying for peak capacity around the clock. Scaling holds performance only when it tracks a metric that reflects real load and handles both scale-out and scale-in without dropping work.

Some workloads run far faster on specialized hardware than on a general-purpose processor. Accelerators, such as GPUs and purpose-built chips, handle massively parallel work such as model training or media processing at a throughput CPUs cannot match. They cost more than general-purpose processors and only pay off when the application offloads work to them and keeps them busy.
