questions.title: How do you select and manage data stores to meet performance requirements?
questions.description: This capability covers how a workload selects and manages data stores for performance: matching each dataset to a purpose-built store, tuning store configuration to the access pattern, measuring store behavior against a baseline, and using query optimization and caching to keep data fast as volume and demand grow.

choices.title: Use a purpose-built data store that best supports your data access and storage requirements

helpfulResource.displayText: Datasets differ in structure, access pattern, and durability. Using one storage technology for every dataset forces trade-offs that degrade performance and raise cost. Match each dataset to a store designed for its characteristics.

improvementPlan.displayText: Use a purpose-built data store that best supports your data access and storage requirements

choices.title: Evaluate available configuration options for data store

helpfulResource.displayText: A data store's default configuration rarely matches a specific workload. Every store exposes options that trade cost, capacity, consistency, and speed against one another. Evaluate and test the configuration before you rely on it.

improvementPlan.displayText: Evaluate available configuration options for data store

choices.title: Collect and record data store performance metrics

helpfulResource.displayText: Without recorded metrics, slow queries and resource pressure in a data store stay invisible until they affect users. Metrics collected over time support data-driven tuning and confirm the store meets workload requirements.

improvementPlan.displayText: Collect and record data store performance metrics

choices.title: Implement strategies to improve query performance in data store

helpfulResource.displayText: To keep a data store efficient and scalable as demand grows, optimize both data layout and query execution.

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement strategies to improve query performance in data store

choices.title: Implement data access patterns that utilize caching

helpfulResource.displayText: You don't need to fetch frequently accessed data from its primary store on every request. A cache keeps a copy closer to the reader, so repeated reads return faster and the primary store carries less load. Caching helps only when the access pattern suits it.

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement data access patterns that utilize caching

questions.title: How do you select and configure networking to meet performance requirements?
questions.description: This capability covers how to design, configure, and operate networking and content delivery for performance: understanding how the network affects the workload, evaluating the features and connectivity options available, distributing traffic, choosing protocols, placing resources close to users and data, and tuning the configuration from telemetry.

helpfulResource.displayText: Networking connects every part of a distributed workload, so network decisions shape latency, throughput, and user experience. Treating a cloud network like an on-premises data center recreates old bottlenecks and wastes capacity.

The cloud exposes network features that reduce latency, shorten the distance traffic travels, and raise throughput. Not every feature helps every workload, and each one adds configuration or cost. When you evaluate features against measured requirements and confirm their impact through testing, you improve performance without adding complexity that does not pay off.

choices.title: Choose appropriate dedicated connectivity or VPN for your workload

helpfulResource.displayText: When a workload spans on-premises and cloud resources, the connection between them becomes a performance boundary. Under-provisioned or poorly chosen hybrid connectivity adds latency and caps throughput for everything that crosses it.

improvementPlan.displayText: Choose appropriate dedicated connectivity or VPN for your workload

choices.title: Use load balancing to distribute traffic across multiple resources

helpfulResource.displayText: Distributing traffic across multiple resources lets a workload scale with demand and stay available when a single resource fails. A load balancer also offloads work such as encryption termination, which frees backend resources to serve requests.

improvementPlan.displayText: Use load balancing to distribute traffic across multiple resources

choices.title: Choose network protocols to improve performance

helpfulResource.displayText: The protocol a workload uses to move data between components shapes the workload's latency, throughput, and reliability. When you match the protocol to each communication requirement, you improve performance and user experience.

improvementPlan.displayText: Choose network protocols to improve performance

choices.title: Choose your workload's location based on network requirements

helpfulResource.displayText: Traffic that crosses continents is slower than traffic served nearby. Placing resources close to users and caching content at the edge reduces page load and data transfer times for remote users.

improvementPlan.displayText: Choose your workload's location based on network requirements

choices.title: Optimize network configuration based on metrics

helpfulResource.displayText: Base your network configuration on measured behavior. When you collect and analyze network telemetry, you can tune configuration to real traffic and confirm each change improves performance.

improvementPlan.displayText: Optimize network configuration based on metrics

questions.title: How do you monitor, test, and improve workload performance over time?
questions.description: The work is continuous and controlled. Instrumentation reveals the components that shape customer experience, testing exposes limits before users reach them, and automation or agents accelerate evidence gathering, triage, and routine low-risk actions. Workload owners retain responsibility for high-impact remediation, update adoption, and changes to monitoring.

choices.title: Use monitoring solutions to understand the areas where performance is most critical

helpfulResource.displayText: Workload components contribute unequally to the customer experience, user-perceived latency, and operating cost. Instrument the workload to reveal those pressure points, and focus optimization on them.

improvementPlan.displayText: Use monitoring solutions to understand the areas where performance is most critical

helpfulResource.displayText: Everyday performance does not predict how a workload behaves at peak traffic. Test the workload against your KPIs under realistic and stressful conditions to find where it slows or stops scaling before customers notice.

choices.title: Use automation to proactively remediate performance-related issues

helpfulResource.displayText: Configure automated investigation as the first line of incident response so analysis starts when an alert or ticket meets your incident criteria. While an engineer responds to the page, the investigation correlates telemetry and topology and returns a root cause or evidence-backed hypotheses. Deterministic automation then handles well-understood, low-risk remediation. Reserve human judgment for uncertain or high-impact actions.

improvementPlan.displayText: Use automation to proactively remediate performance-related issues

choices.title: Keep your workload and services up-to-date

helpfulResource.displayText: Cloud providers regularly release new services, instance types, and features, and many can deliver better price-performance for what you already run. Review new releases and adopt the ones that benefit your workload.

improvementPlan.displayText: Keep your workload and services up-to-date

helpfulResource.displayText: The metrics that matter change as the workload evolves. Traffic patterns shift, components change, and thresholds that once signaled trouble fire on normal behavior. Review metrics and alarms on a regular cadence and after significant incidents or workload changes.

questions.title: How do you implement cloud financial management?
questions.description: Cost is a shared responsibility across finance, engineering, and business teams. You need a shared vocabulary, a single source of cost metrics, and a regular review cadence. This capability describes how those teams plan and govern spend together.

helpfulResource.displayText: Because cloud spending changes with usage, adapt your budgeting, forecasting, and financial planning for variable, usage-based costs. Combine historical usage trends with business events to project future spend.
Set goals that state the outcome your organization expects, and set targets that make each goal specific, measurable, and time-bound. Teams can then track progress and hold themselves accountable.

A project ends, a workload moves to production, an experiment concludes, yet the environments behind them keep running and costing money. Track the lifecycle of projects, teams, and environments so you can decommission or resize resources that no longer serve an active need.

choices.title: Keep up-to-date with new service releases

helpfulResource.displayText: Cloud providers release new services, features, and price reductions constantly. Each release can make part of your architecture cheaper to run, and each price cut can change a decision you made months ago. Staying current, through your own monitoring and through experts who track the cloud provider, turns these changes into recurring savings.

improvementPlan.displayText: Keep up-to-date with new service releases

helpfulResource.displayText: Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you monitor your cost and usage?
questions.description: Cost visibility is a shared responsibility. Engineering decisions to provision and operate resources create spend, so cost data must reach those engineers in a form they can use. This capability describes how an organization builds that visibility and keeps it accurate as the environment grows.

choices.title: Implement granular resource tagging for workload cost allocation

helpfulResource.displayText: Label each resource with a consistent set of tags so cost traces back to the team, product, or environment that owns it. Without tagging, spend collapses into service-and-account totals that no team can act on.

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement granular resource tagging for workload cost allocation

choices.title: Allocate costs based on workload metrics and business outcomes

helpfulResource.displayText: To measure workload efficiency, tie spend to a business outcome, such as an order, a report, or an active user. Cost per outcome then shows whether the workload gets cheaper or more expensive as it grows.

improvementPlan.displayText: Allocate costs based on workload metrics and business outcomes

helpfulResource.displayText: Waiting for the monthly invoice means an inefficiency has already run for weeks before anyone sees it. Proactive monitoring reviews cost and usage on a regular cadence and surfaces changes as they happen. The goal is to make spend visible to the teams that create it, as well as the teams that pay for it.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you manage the lifecycle of your resources?
questions.description: Lifecycle management matters more as a workload scales, because manual cleanup does not keep pace with resources that automation creates, replicates, and clones. Systematic tracking, scheduled review, and automated retention turn cleanup into an ongoing routine, so spend follows business value.

helpfulResource.displayText: Track each resource from provisioning to retirement so you can retire it when its purpose ends. Consistent tracking makes cleanup a routine you can automate.

When a workload changes, some resources become oversized, idle, or obsolete, and keep running until someone acts. Efficient lifecycle management matches capacity to real demand and retires resources you no longer need, through scaling and decommissioning triggered on a schedule or by events.

Every object, backup, snapshot, and log you keep occupies storage you pay for, and much of it outlives its usefulness. Data retention policies define how long each type of data must be kept and when to move it to cheaper storage or delete it. Automating those policies controls storage cost and improves your ability to meet retention requirements.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you plan for and optimize data transfer costs?
questions.description: This capability covers documenting how data moves across services and environments, modeling transfer cost before deployment, and revisiting the design as pricing and usage change. Data transfer is entangled with performance, reliability, and security, so decisions here weigh cost against the resilience and latency that traffic patterns provide. Avoid defaulting to the cheapest path.

choices.title: Define network and data transfer infrastructure costs

helpfulResource.displayText: Data transfer cost depends on the path traffic takes through your network, and shared network components spread those charges across many workloads. Document your network architecture and the transfer pricing that applies to each path so you can attribute cost to the workloads that drive it.

improvementPlan.displayText: Define network and data transfer infrastructure costs

helpfulResource.displayText: Data transfer is a significant part of a workload's cost. What you pay depends on where data moves, how often, and how those patterns change as the workload grows. Model data transfer during design to compare architectural options on cost alongside performance and resilience.

choices.title: Optimize services to reduce data transfer costs

helpfulResource.displayText: Pricing, service capabilities, and your usage patterns change over time. Optimize data transfer continuously to keep cost proportional to value while preserving performance, reliability, and security.

improvementPlan.displayText: Optimize services to reduce data transfer costs

helpfulResource.displayText: Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you evaluate cost when you select services?
questions.description: Good selection is comprehensive, data-driven, and proportional. It weighs every component and its dependencies, rests on actual and projected usage, and matches the effort of each analysis to the savings it can produce. It is also collaborative and continuous where technical, financial, and business stakeholders share the trade-offs, and choices are reassessed as workloads and available services change.

helpfulResource.displayText: Cost competes with performance, reliability, delivery speed, and team familiarity, and the right balance differs for every workload. Capture these priorities and the trade-offs behind them before you select services, then revisit them as the business changes.

choices.title: Analyze all components of the workload

helpfulResource.displayText: A workload has many components, and small ones add up as usage grows. Review every component, and scale review depth to potential savings.

improvementPlan.displayText: Analyze all components of the workload

choices.title: Analyze the total cost of ownership of each component

helpfulResource.displayText: A component's total cost includes more than its list price. Running it yourself adds operational work: patching, scaling, monitoring, incident response, and the staff hours to do it. Count these hidden costs when you compare managed and self-managed options, so the comparison reflects the real total.

improvementPlan.displayText: Analyze the total cost of ownership of each component

helpfulResource.displayText: Software licenses can rival infrastructure as a share of workload cost. Licenses tied to fixed attributes such as processor cores penalize cloud elasticity, because you pay for capacity whether it produces value. Favor open-source options and licenses priced by usage or business outcome, so licensing cost scales with the value the software delivers.

choices.title: Select components for business-value-driven cost optimization

helpfulResource.displayText: Managed and serverless options remove idle capacity and operational overhead, event-driven designs do work only when required, and open-source software avoids license fees. Weigh these choices against the business value each component delivers.

improvementPlan.displayText: Select components for business-value-driven cost optimization

helpfulResource.displayText: Usage patterns shift, workloads grow, and new service options appear, so a one-time review drifts out of date. Treat cost analysis as an ongoing practice that combines forecasts, continuous monitoring, and scheduled reviews.
Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: How do you meet cost targets when you select resource type, size, and number?
questions.description: Right-sizing is both an initial design decision and an ongoing discipline. A resource that fits at launch drifts out of fit as demand cycles, data ages, and usage grows. Revisit the choice as the workload runs. Match right-sizing effort to a workload's cost impact: analyze high-cost resources more deeply than low-cost ones.

helpfulResource.displayText: Cost modeling estimates the cost of a workload and each of its components under expected load before you commit to a configuration. Model the components that carry the most cost or risk first, so the effort matches the potential return.

choices.title: Select resource type, size, and number based on data

helpfulResource.displayText: Base the type, size, and number of resources on evidence of the workload's compute, memory, throughput, and storage demands. Draw that evidence from a prior version of the workload, vendor documentation, published benchmarks, or a cost model.

improvementPlan.displayText: Select resource type, size, and number based on data

choices.title: Select resource type, size, and number automatically based on metrics

helpfulResource.displayText: Use metrics from the running workload to adjust resource type, size, and number as conditions shift. Drive these adjustments through a feedback loop, such as managed automatic scaling, automatic storage tiering, or custom code in the workload.

improvementPlan.displayText: Select resource type, size, and number automatically based on metrics

helpfulResource.displayText: Common functions duplicated across teams multiply cost without adding value. When multiple business units need the same capability, such as monitoring, backups, directory services, or connectivity, a shared resource raises utilization and lowers total cost of ownership. Consolidation only pays off when you allocate the shared cost back to the teams that consume it.

questions.title: How do you use pricing models to reduce cost?
questions.description: Steady, long-running components benefit from commitment-based discounts, while short-lived or elastic components are cheaper on usage-based or interruptible models. Match components to models by measuring how they run, and revisit the choice as demand shifts.

helpfulResource.displayText: Workload components differ in how long they run, how predictable their usage is, and whether they tolerate interruption. Match each component to the pricing model that suits its usage pattern, and revisit the match as demand changes.

Resource prices vary by Region. Where latency, data residency, data sovereignty, and regulatory rules permit, placing a workload in a lower-cost Region reduces spend. Data transfer costs and service availability can outweigh the price difference.

choices.title: Select third-party agreements with cost-efficient terms

helpfulResource.displayText: Choose agreements whose cost scales with the benefit they deliver, keeping cost justified as your usage grows.

improvementPlan.displayText: Select third-party agreements with cost-efficient terms

questions.title: How do you plan for and supply resources to match demand?
questions.description: Demand rarely arrives at a steady rate, and the right response depends on its shape. Predictable, time-based patterns call for a different approach than sharp, variable spikes. When you can smooth demand at the edge through buffering or throttling, capacity tracks average demand instead of peak. When you cannot, provisioning must adjust to demand automatically. The best practices under this capability describe how to analyze demand, smooth it, and supply resources to meet what remains.

choices.title: Perform an analysis on the workload demand

helpfulResource.displayText: A workload's resource needs rise and fall with usage. Match provisioned capacity to that demand to control cost while meeting performance targets. Focus analysis on workloads where demand varies most and costs the most.

improvementPlan.displayText: Perform an analysis on the workload demand

choices.title: Implement a buffer or throttle to manage demand

helpfulResource.displayText: Demand rarely arrives at a steady rate. When a workload provisions capacity for every peak, that capacity sits idle between peaks. You pay for the peak, even though average demand is lower. Buffering and throttling smooth the incoming rate so the workload runs closer to average demand. Buffering stores requests for later processing, while throttling asks clients to slow down and retry.

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement a buffer or throttle to manage demand

helpfulResource.displayText: With static capacity, you either pay for peak demand around the clock or you fail when demand climbs past what you provisioned. Deploying resources dynamically avoids both problems by adjusting capacity as demand changes. Some demand is predictable by time of day or week. The rest varies with real-time conditions. Match the provisioning method to the type of demand.

questions.title: How do you evaluate new services and optimize over time?
questions.description: Match review frequency to each workload's share of spend. Perform quarterly or bi-annual deep reviews for workloads representing more than roughly 10 percent of cost. Review lower-impact workloads annually.

helpfulResource.displayText: Cloud services, pricing models, and architectural patterns change. A workload that was cost-optimized last year might not be optimized today, and a single optimization can't keep pace. A repeatable review process finds savings on a cadence that matches each workload's cost and importance.

choices.title: Continuously review and optimize the workload

helpfulResource.displayText: Cloud providers release new services, features, and pricing models continuously. Each release can make part of your workload cheaper to run. A workload you never revisit drifts from the most cost-effective design. Continuous review turns those releases into savings: decide whether to adopt new capabilities, replace components, or keep the current design.

improvementPlan.displayText: Continuously review and optimize the workload

questions.title: How do you automate operations to optimize cost?
questions.description: Automation itself takes engineering time to build, test, and maintain. The tasks worth automating repeat often, take a long time, or fail expensively by hand. Natural-language tools can also shorten cost analysis. Teams query spend and identify optimization opportunities faster, and a person reviews the resulting decisions before acting.

helpfulResource.displayText: Repetitive tasks such as provisioning, configuration, patching, monitoring, and cleanup consume engineering time and introduce errors that raise cost. Automate them to lower operational overhead, make cost control repeatable, and free your teams for higher-value work.

choices.title: Use generative AI services and solutions for efficiency

helpfulResource.displayText: Cost management generates a large amount of data that your teams must interpret and act on. Generative AI can shorten that work. It answers questions in natural language, summarizes spend, and surfaces optimization opportunities that would take an analyst hours to find. With clear goals and human review, it makes routine cost analysis faster.

questions.title: How do you measure, monitor, and account for the sustainability impact of your workload?
questions.description: Together, RUE and carbon emissions data help you understand your resource usage and its relative carbon impact. As detailed in the methodology, emissions in AWS Sustainability depend on your usage. Track workload RUE and emissions over time to observe how efficiency gains and changes in your workload demand influence your emissions.

helpfulResource.displayText: Resource usage efficiency (RUE) provides an essential baseline for understanding your workload's resource intensity (which links to Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions) by helping you calculate an efficiency metric for your workload. RUE is calculated by dividing the core resource provisioned metric (which could be volume of storage or normalized instance hours) by the amount of work completed (measured by a business metric or customer outcome). Track RUE over time to establish clear baselines, set improvement targets, and validate the effectiveness of your sustainability initiatives and optimization efforts.

choices.title: Create dashboards to combine resource usage efficiency and environmental impact data

helpfulResource.displayText: The carbon emissions associated with your AWS usage are influenced by several factors, including the resources you have provisioned to support your workload. Efficient use of resources reduces the environmental impact of your workload and is directly correlated with the emissions associated with the workload. Create dashboards that visualize your resource usage efficiency (RUE) alongside data from the AWS Sustainability service to provide a holistic view of your cloud workload's environmental impact. Dashboards should showcase RUE and workload environmental impact.

improvementPlan.displayText: Create dashboards to combine resource usage efficiency and environmental impact data

choices.title: Select Regions that align to your sustainability goals

helpfulResource.displayText: While many factors influence Region selection, incorporating sustainability into your decision-making can support your environmental goals. Choose an AWS Region by first evaluating essential requirements such as cost, latency, service availability, and compliance. Then, from the shortlisted Regions that meet these criteria, consider the carbon intensity of each Region's power grid to make an environmentally conscious decision.

improvementPlan.displayText: Select Regions that align to your sustainability goals

questions.title: How do you provision resources to match workload demand and avoid waste?
questions.description: Optimizing resource provisioning means that you allocate only the resources needed for your workloads, reducing waste and improving efficiency. This section covers using reserved capacity for predictable workloads, implementing elasticity through auto-scaling, event-driven invocation, and serverless technologies for variable workloads, dynamically provisioning development environments to eliminate idle resources during non-working hours, and matching resource allocation precisely to business requirements to avoid over-provisioning.

helpfulResource.displayText: For workloads with variable or unpredictable demand, implement elasticity through serverless technologies and auto-scaling capabilities to allow your infrastructure to dynamically adjust to actual demand. This approach verifies that resources are only consumed when needed and automatically scaled back during periods of low activity, significantly reducing idle capacity and wasted resources.

choices.title: Provision development, build, and test resources dynamically

helpfulResource.displayText: Workloads use non-production resources intermittently and for a limited amount of time along the development lifecycle. Examples are developers' workstations, compute instances for builds, user acceptance tests, and pre-production environments. To reduce the resource consumption of your software development lifecycle, maintain development and test resources only when actively needed, rather than keeping them permanently provisioned. By using automation to create and decommission environments on demand, resources are only consumed during active development and testing phases.

improvementPlan.displayText: Provision development, build, and test resources dynamically

choices.title: Match resource use to business need

helpfulResource.displayText: Designing customer experience with sustainability in mind involves making intentional trade-offs that can significantly reduce resource consumption while maintaining acceptable service levels. Align service-level objectives (SLOs) with your real business requirements to produce an efficient system.

improvementPlan.displayText: Match resource use to business need

choices.title: Define the baseload for predictable and steady-state workloads

helpfulResource.displayText: Most workloads combine two kinds of demand: a steady-state baseload that runs continuously, and variable demand that rises and falls on top of that baseload. Handle variable demand with elasticity, as described in SUS02-BP01. You pay for an oversized baseline every hour of every day, so the same percentage of waste costs far more resource over a year in the baseload than in a component that runs briefly.

improvementPlan.displayText: Define the baseload for predictable and steady-state workloads

questions.title: How do you improve the resource efficiency of your workload?
questions.description: This capability covers best practices to enhance workload efficiency. The cloud is inherently flexible, and you can provision resources as needed. Be intentional about your choices and usage of AWS services, resources, and features. It is important that you continually evaluate your design decisions, and explore opportunities to maximize efficiency and decommission unused resources.

choices.title: Optimize workloads for high resource usage efficiency

helpfulResource.displayText: Optimizing workloads to use resources efficiently and eliminate waste is fundamental to sustainable cloud operations. By implementing a cycle of measurement, optimization, and validation, you can identify and eliminate inefficiencies such as idle resources, over-provisioning, or inefficient processes. The goal is to maximize the business value per resource consumed, reducing both environmental impact and operational costs.

improvementPlan.displayText: Optimize workloads for high resource usage efficiency

choices.title: Flatten demand peaks for consistently high resource utilization

helpfulResource.displayText: When demand is unpredictable and spiky, provision enough capacity to meet peak loads. Techniques such as buffering and throttling smooth out the load and maintain a consistently high level of resource utilization, reducing the need for excess capacity to handle peaks and improving overall efficiency. By transforming spiky workload patterns into steadier, more predictable ones, you can provision resources that operate at high utilization and resource efficiency levels most of the time.

improvementPlan.displayText: Flatten demand peaks for consistently high resource utilization

choices.title: Use the most resource-efficient computational approach

helpfulResource.displayText: Choosing the right computational approach, from simple code to agentic AI, can impact the resource efficiency of your workload. While agentic AI can provide powerful capabilities for complex problems, it often requires more computational resources than traditional algorithmic approaches, which may be more efficient for problems where rules can be explicitly defined. Decide when to use machine learning or traditional algorithms based on the nature of the problem, data availability, and resource implications. By selecting the most appropriate approach for each use case, you minimize unnecessary resource consumption while achieving your desired outcomes.

improvementPlan.displayText: Use the most resource-efficient computational approach

choices.title: Use purpose-built, energy efficient hardware tailored to your workload

helpfulResource.displayText: Software optimizations have diminishing returns when the underlying hardware isn't matched to the workload. AWS offers managed service features and Amazon EC2 instance types to tailor the underlying hardware involved to the processing needs of a workload. For example, you can select several types of CPU architecture, purpose-built silicon for machine learning, instance storage options, or network adapter features. By selecting the right features for your workload, you can optimize the use of resources and energy and lower your environmental impact for workloads that are compute, storage, or network-bound while simultaneously improving performance and reducing costs.

improvementPlan.displayText: Use purpose-built, energy efficient hardware tailored to your workload

questions.title: How do you manage data and processing to minimize resource use?
questions.description: Efficient data management and processing affect sustainability by reducing unnecessary storage and computational requirements. Implement data lifecycle policies to eliminate redundant or obsolete data. Select file formats and compression techniques that minimize storage while maintaining functionality. Design distributed systems thoughtfully, placing processing close to data and optimizing resource use across your architecture.

helpfulResource.displayText: Eliminate data that no longer serves a business purpose. Whether redundant, obsolete, trivial, or simply unknown - aim to reduce storage requirements and the associated environmental impact of your workload.

choices.title: Select appropriate file formats, compression, and software implementation

helpfulResource.displayText: Designing efficient distributed systems requires careful consideration of both what components should be distributed and where they should be located. Properly architected distributed systems can significantly reduce resource consumption by placing processing close to data, minimizing data movement, and optimizing communication patterns between components.
